cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf varieties (for Dianqing and pu-erh)
processing: Fresh leaf is fixed and rolled, then dried in sunlight rather than baked or pan-fired. Much of it stays as rough maocha, the raw material for pressed teas.
harvest_season: Varies by region. In Yunnan, as for pu-erh raw material generally, spring is the prized picking.
appearance_dry: Sturdy, thick strands with some white down showing.
taste_profile: Rich and mellow with strong astringency and a distinct sun-dried aroma; it holds up well across many steeps.

brewing.notes: Short gongfu steeps tame the astringency. Treat it more like young raw pu-erh than a delicate spring green.

vintage_note: As loose maocha it is bought by harvest season, usually the most recent one. Most sun-dried green tea is pressed into tuo, brick or pu-erh forms, and those are then sold by production year and may be kept for ageing, as raw pu-erh is.
description:
Shaiqing is the sun-dried branch of Chinese green tea, one of the four standard groups alongside pan-fired, baked and steamed. Its most famous form is Dianqing from Yunnan, and it matters far beyond its own cup, since pu-erh starts here.

After fixing and rolling, the leaf dries in sunlight. That slower, gentler finish leaves a thick, sturdy strand and a recognisable sun-dried smell that baked and wok-finished greens do not have.

Expect a stronger drink than a typical green tea: full, mellow and quite astringent, with lots of steeps in it. Long steeps at boiling point are the common mistake; short ones show the sweetness under the grip.

Some shaiqing is drunk loose, but most ends up pressed into tuo, brick or raw pu-erh. Only tea made from Yunnan large-leaf sun-dried maocha is pu-erh in the formal sense, so a sun-dried green from elsewhere is not pu-erh, whatever its shape. Sipping a loose Dianqing is a good way to learn what raw pu-erh is before pressing and time.
history:
Sun-drying is among the simplest ways to finish tea, and producers and writers often describe it as an old method: leaf lightly fired, rolled and left in the sun. No single origin is documented.

The method's modern importance comes from Yunnan, where large-leaf sun-dried maocha is the defined raw material of pu-erh, both raw and ripe.
